work.headingAccent: One audit, one agent, and the run cost quoted before you commit to either.
work.s1Desc: What is expensive, what is repetitive, and where the data actually lives. Most of what we learn in this call is whether there is a build here at all, and sometimes the answer is no.
work.s2Desc: We look at your data and your process, not your slides. We come back with the one thing worth automating, why the other candidates are traps, and what each would cost to run per month.
work.s3Tag: the audit fee comes off it
work.s3Desc: What it does, what it costs to build, what it costs to run, and the date it ships. If the audit finds nothing worth building, we tell you that and you keep the report anyway.
work.s4Title: We build it, with evals from day one
work.s4Desc: The eval set exists before the agent does. That is the difference between an agent that got better and an agent that felt better, and it is the only way either of us knows which one we have.
work.s5Title: Guardrails and tracing, before a customer sees it
work.s5Desc: Prompt injection, PII leakage, hallucination, off-topic drift. Every run traced. An agent is a distributed system where the model happens to be the planner, and it needs to be observable like one.
work.s6Desc: The code is in your repository and the infrastructure is in your account, from day one. If you want us to run it afterwards, we will quote that separately, and you are free to say no.

faq.subtitle: Including the ones about what we do not have.
faq.q1: What does <brand></brand> actually deliver, and who owns it?
faq.a1: One agent that removes a named cost, together with the things that make it safe to put in front of a customer: an eval suite, guardrails, tracing, and a quoted monthly running cost. The code lives in your repository and the infrastructure in your account from the first day, not handed over at the end as a favour.
faq.q2: What does it cost to RUN per month, not to build?
faq.a2: We quote that before you commit to the build, and there is a calculator on this page that does it in front of you. This is the question a general development shop cannot answer, and it matters because the initial build is only about a quarter to a third of a three-year total cost of ownership. Whoever ignores the other two thirds is not being careless, they are being quiet.
faq.q3: How do you test something that is not deterministic?
faq.a3: With an eval set built before the agent, and by testing the whole trajectory rather than the final answer: did it pick the right tool, did it call it with the right arguments, did it stop when it should have. An agent that gives the right answer through the wrong path will fail differently tomorrow, and a test that only checks the answer will not tell you.
faq.q4: What if it hallucinates in front of my customer?
faq.a4: Then either the retrieval failed or there is no guardrail, and both are our fault rather than the model's. Grounding, citations, refusal behaviour and an output check are part of the build, not an upgrade. We will also tell you honestly where the residual risk is, because it is never zero and anyone who says otherwise has not shipped one of these.
faq.q5: Do you train on my data? Where does it go?
faq.a5: No, and we will put it in writing. Where it goes depends on what you can live with: a hosted model, a European region, or entirely inside your own infrastructure. That last option costs more and removes an entire category of argument with your legal team, and for some companies that trade is obviously worth it.
faq.q6: How do you scope it if I do not know what I want yet?
faq.a6: That is what the audit is for, and it is why it exists as a paid, fixed, five-day thing rather than a free discovery call that quietly turns into a proposal. Five days of us in your data is worth more to you than five weeks of us guessing.
faq.q7: Is the audit fee really credited against the build?
faq.a7: In full. And if the audit concludes there is no build worth doing, we say so, you keep the report, and we have both saved a great deal of money. That happens, and it is not a failure of the audit, it is the audit working.
faq.q8: What if we go over the fixed price? Who eats it?
faq.a8: We do, within the scope we agreed. What we will not do is absorb a scope change and pretend it was always in there, because that is how agencies quietly turn a fixed price into a fight. Changes are priced when they happen, in front of you.
faq.q9: Why you and not Cursor plus our own intern?
faq.a9: For a prototype, genuinely, use Cursor and your intern. We would. The difference appears the day it faces a customer: evals, guardrails, tracing, cost control, and someone whose job it is when it breaks. If nobody is going to be harmed by a wrong answer, you probably do not need us, and we will say so on the call.
faq.q10: Why you and not a 25 dollar an hour outsourcing shop?
faq.a10: For a CRUD app, no reason at all, and we would lose that comparison on price and deserve to. An agent is not a CRUD app. It is non-deterministic, it costs money every time it thinks, and it can be talked into things. The shop that has never built an eval set will hand you something that demos beautifully and cannot be trusted, and you will not find out for three months.
faq.a11: No, and we are not going to invent any. This is a new arm of an existing agency, and a page claiming five hundred projects and ninety-eight percent satisfaction is a page you should distrust on principle. What we have instead is a fixed-price audit, which is a cheap way for you to find out whether we can think, and which costs you nothing if the answer is that there is no work here.
faq.q12: Do you hold SOC2 or ISO certification?
faq.a12: No. If your procurement requires it, we are not your vendor this year, and we would rather tell you now than waste a quarter of your time discovering it in a questionnaire.
faq.q13: Can you integrate with our existing systems?
faq.a13: Usually, and the audit is where we find out honestly rather than optimistically. The systems that break this are the ones with no API and a database schema last documented by someone who left in 2019, and if that is yours, we will tell you what it will really take.
faq.q14: aiAPP or vibecoding.ge. Which one do I need?
faq.a14: aiAPP builds. If what you have is an app that was already built with an AI tool and it is now broken, leaking, or failing a technical due diligence, that is a different job with a different method and it lives at vibecoding.ge.

eval.heading: The eval suite. This is the part nobody else hands you.
eval.subtitle: A dev shop ships you an agent. We ship you the thing that tells you whether the agent is getting better or just getting different.
eval.why: Why a trajectory and not just the answer
eval.whyBody: An agent that reaches the right answer through the wrong tool will fail differently tomorrow. A test that only checks the final string will not tell you that, and by the time it matters, it will be in front of a customer.
eval.injectionBody: The test case tries to talk the agent into ignoring its instructions and dumping its context. The guardrail stops it before the model ever sees it. This case is in the suite from day one, not added after the incident.
eval.note: An illustrative run. On your build the cases are yours, the numbers are yours, and you watch them move.

cost.eyebrow: The number a dev shop cannot give you
cost.heading: What does it cost to run, per month?
cost.subtitle: Not what it costs to build. That is the question everyone asks, and it is the smaller half of the bill.
cost.shareOf: of what you will actually spend
cost.reveal: Initial development is only about a quarter to a third of a three-year total cost of ownership, an industry finding we did not measure ourselves. It is the reason we quote both numbers before you commit to either.
cost.note: Token prices move. This is arithmetic on today's public rates, not a quote, and your real number lands in the audit.

ladder.heading: Three rungs. You can stop after the first.
ladder.subtitle: Click a rung.
ladder.r1what: We look at your data and your process. You get the one thing worth building, why the others are traps, what each costs to run per month, and a fixed price and date for the build.
ladder.r1risk: If we find nothing worth building, we say so and you keep the report. You have spent 1,500 dollars to avoid spending fifty thousand.
ladder.r2what: One agent, with the eval suite, the guardrails and the tracing. Code in your repository, infrastructure in your account, from day one.
ladder.r2risk: The audit fee comes off this. So the audit was free if you build, and cheap if you do not.
ladder.r3what: We operate it, watch the evals, keep the cost down as your traffic grows, and answer when it breaks.
ladder.r3risk: Optional. It is your code and your infrastructure, so you can take it in-house whenever you want, and we will help you do that rather than make it difficult.
ladder.note: There are only two prices on this page and one of them refunds itself.

proof.note: A test that only checks the final answer will not tell you the agent reached it down the wrong path. That is what a dev shop hands you.
